title: Dash: RAG plus code-planned agents for universal business search
problem: Business knowledge is scattered across apps, formats and modalities, slowing search and raising access-control risk.
depth: Detailed design rationale and trade-offs; no model names or accuracy figures
technologies_stated: LLM-planned code in a Python-like DSL
facts: Dropbox chose a traditional lexical index with embedding-based reranking over a pure vector index.
For complex tasks an LLM expresses a plan as code in a Python-like DSL which a purpose-built minimal interpreter validates with static analysis and dry runs.
The interpreter implements only required functionality to reduce the risks of a full-featured interpreter.
The post names trade-offs: latency versus quality, freshness versus scalability, budget versus experience, model size versus latency and accuracy.
Evaluation uses public datasets plus LLM judges for correctness and completeness and passage-level precision, recall and F1.
The post reports over 95% of queries completing in 1-2 seconds.
Prompts do not transfer cleanly between models.
interpretations: Planning as code makes failures locatable and testable, giving determinism that free-form tool loops lack.
unknown: Model names, embedding model, index technology
How permissions are enforced inside retrieval and agent execution

decisions.alternatives: Pure vector index; pure lexical search
decisions.reasoning: Source states these as trade-offs; detailed reasoning is limited.

decisions.selected: LLM-written code in a restricted DSL executed by a custom interpreter
decisions.alternatives: Iterative tool calling; general-purpose Python sandbox; fixed workflows
decisions.reasoning: Source describes the DSL approach and its security benefit of a minimal interpreter; alternatives comparison is independent analysis.

decisions.selected: Periodic sync with webhooks where appropriate, query-time chunking
decisions.alternatives: Live API calls per query; full real-time indexing
decisions.reasoning: Source discusses the freshness versus scalability trade-off.

review_exercise: The post does not say how access control is enforced during retrieval and agent execution. Propose three enforcement points and the failure each prevents.
lessons: Restrict what an agent can express, not just what it may call.
Make retrieval model-agnostic and measure it end to end.
adaptation: Applies to cross-system SAP CX search (Commerce, Sales, Service content) where permission models differ per source. Independent analysis.
